entry.evidence: Very little is known how basin-wide development and climate change would impact the Cambodian Mekong floodplain other than the Tonle Sap

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), with PDF for figures

steps.action: Take projected basin-scale flow changes under climate change, hydropower and irrigation from published model studies (Hoang et al. 2016, 2019; Lauri et al. 2012) as expectations.
steps.quote: hydropower development plans in the Mekong River basin are expected to increase dry season flows up to + 133 %

steps.action: Name the gap that the Cambodian Mekong floodplain outside the Tonle Sap is unstudied, and set the aim of quantifying the cumulative impacts of development plans and climate change there.
steps.quote: Very little is known how basin-wide development and climate change would impact the Cambodian Mekong floodplain other than the Tonle Sap

steps.action: Design a three-model chain: basin hydrology (IWRM-VMod, 5 km) drives 1D delta propagation (MIKE 11, with sea level), which supplies boundary conditions to the 2D floodplain model (IWRM-Sub, 1 km).
steps.quote: We used a hydrological–floodplain model combination (Fig. 2), consisting of the distributed hydrological model IWRM-VMod

steps.action: Reuse the basin-wide baseline and scenario runs of the co-authors' earlier study (Hoang et al. 2019), and MIKE 11 as built in Triet et al. (2017, 2020).
steps.quote: We used the model runs, both baseline and scenarios, from Hoang et al. (2019).

steps.action: Check the CMIP5 climate forcing premise by comparing CMIP5 and CMIP6 seasonal mean precipitation and temperature over the study area (Supplement Table S1).
steps.quote: an analysis of the differences between model collections shows consistent mean values for both precipitation and temperature across our study area

steps.action: Recalibrate the floodplain model setup for the 1971-2000 baseline against discharge and water level at four stations, scored with NSE, PBIAS, RSR and R2.
steps.quote: which we further calibrated and validated against observations of water discharge and water level taken at Kratie, Kampong Cham, Chroy Changvar, and Neak Loeung

steps.action: Derive observed flood extent maps from a 1984-2000 Landsat 4/5 stack with the Surface Water Mapping Tool (MNDWI, HAND correction).
steps.quote: A stack of Landsat (4 and 5) data were generated using SWMT from 1984–2000.

steps.action: Adopt the twelve-scenario design of Hoang et al. (2019): drivers alone and combined, 5 GCMs, RCP4.5/8.5 for 2036-2065, 126 dams, two irrigation expansions, and sea level +43 cm taken from Manh et al. (2015).
steps.quote: The scenario setup that we adopted for our study is the same as that described in Hoang et al. (2019).

steps.action: Validate IWRM-Sub against gauge records (Table 3, Figs. S2-S3) and against SWMT satellite flood extent (ratio, recall, precision; Fig. 3). The upstream models' validations from earlier studies are cited, not repeated.
steps.quote: a good model performance is obtained at all stations (both water discharge and water level)

steps.action: Attribute the roughly 29% non-overlap between simulated and observed extents partly to rivers and lakes being included only in the simulation, and keep the setup as not unduly affected by compounding errors.
steps.quote: Part of this discrepancy may be accounted for by the inclusion of rivers and lakes in the extent of the simulation

steps.action: Run all scenarios S1-S12 through the chain, with inflow modulated at Kratie and the Tonle Sap confluence, and compute percentage changes in mean monthly discharge and water level per station.
steps.quote: Having run the model for each of the development scenarios (S1–S12; see Table 2), we obtained the corresponding daily time series of water discharge

steps.action: Compare the scenario hydrographs with the baseline at Kampong Cham and Neak Loeung: hydropower raises dry-season flows (up to about 150% in water level) and lowers early wet-season flows, while climate change partly offsets it in the wet months.
steps.quote: All scenarios that contain an element of hydropower development follow the same pattern of increasing both water discharge and water level during the dry season

steps.action: Simulate the baseline yearly flooded area for 1971-2000 (7785-11 525 km2, mean 9370 km2).
steps.quote: Its mean annual value is estimated at 9370 km2, about 34 % of the whole study area.

steps.action: Compare year-by-year flooded area and spatial depth and duration changes against the baseline: hydropower alone gives a median reduction above 20%, combined scenarios up to 40%, climate alone an increase.
steps.quote: there is a clear pattern that emerges, once again showing the dominance of hydropower development in significantly reducing the yearly flooded area

steps.action: Simulate baseline flooded area, depth and duration for ten provinces.
steps.quote: the average flooded area ranges from a minimum of 188 km2 in Phnom Penh Province to a maximum of 2308 km2 in Prey Veng Province

steps.action: Compare provincial scenario changes with the baseline: Prey Veng and Takéo are most affected by climate change, and Svay Rieng shows anomalous shorter, deeper floods.
steps.quote: Kampong Chhnang and Kratie are least affected by the impacts of climate change, whilst Prey Veng and Takéo are most affected (Fig. 7)

steps.action: Set the baseline performance metrics and the projected trends against earlier regional studies; the metrics exceed most and the trends agree with most.
steps.quote: exceed existing studies within the same region (Västilä et al., 2010), with the exception of Dang [...] )

steps.action: Keep the claim that planned hydropower will homogenize the hydrograph and dominate irrigation and climate effects, reducing flood extent.
steps.quote: Our findings clearly demonstrate the homogenizing effect that the planned hydropower developments would have on the Mekong River's hydrograph

steps.action: Keep the three-model setup as validated and transferable to other large-river floodplains.
steps.quote: We show through model validation that the developed modelling setup performs well in the study area

steps.action: Restructure the scenarios so that each development driver is run with and without climate change, and climate change alone, using the Hoang et al. (2019) and Triet et al. (2020) data.
steps.quote: we will consider each with and without the impact of climate change, as well as climate change in isolation

steps.action: Change the baseline to 1971-2000. The referee asked for more recent years; the authors chose an older, less-altered period for separability and comparability.
steps.quote: For our new set of scenarios, we will actually use a slightly older baseline (1971 – 2001).

steps.action: Replace the single GCM with a five-GCM CMIP5 ensemble at two RCPs, and add a CMIP5 versus CMIP6 comparison to the supplement.
steps.quote: we will add an analysis to the supplementary of the differences in projected precipitation and temperature between CMIP5 and CMIP6

steps.action: Decline to replace the SRTM 90 m DEM with MERIT, citing model construction. A comparison was promised but does not appear in the published paper.
steps.quote: unfortunately we cannot change the underlying DEM

steps.action: Replace the simpler delta flood model with MIKE 11 covering the Vietnamese delta, bringing sea level and delta processes in through boundary conditions, after the referee's transboundary critique.
steps.quote: the simpler flood model used previously will be changed to MIKE 11, that covers the processes in Vietnam delta very well

steps.action: Defend the four calibration stations and promise to explore adding Prek Kdam on the Tonle Sap River. The published paper still uses four stations.
steps.quote: These four stations were used, as they have good data coverage.

tree.answer: Projected change in floodplain hydrology and flooding under development and climate scenarios around 2050
No; future conditions. Only the baseline is observed (gauges, Landsat).
Quantify the cumulative and individual driver impacts on discharge, water level and flood extent, depth and duration
No rival hypotheses; driver scenarios (hydropower, irrigation, climate) are run alone and combined
Scenarios yield distinct seasonal and flood-extent signatures
Set in the model via scenario boundary conditions
Baseline validated against gauges and satellite extent; CMIP5/CMIP6 input check; no parameter sensitivity tests
Kept: hydropower dominates; flood extent declines by about 20%
Major revision: scenarios restructured, five-GCM and two-RCP ensemble, MIKE 11 added; DEM change declined

end.claim: Planned hydropower development will drastically alter Mekong mainstream hydrology (dry-season flows up to +140%, early wet-season flows up to -30%) and reduce floodplain flood extent by about 20%, outweighing irrigation and climate-change effects.

decisive_move.sentence: Running the twelve scenarios through the validated three-model chain produces every projected change the claim rests on.

gates.evidence: Action: no hypothesis directed data acquisition; the scenarios and basin runs were inherited from Hoang et al. (2019) (§2.4 ¶1). Claim: only the baseline faced a failable test (Table 3 against literature guideline thresholds; satellite extent §3.1 ¶3), while the projections themselves cannot be tested. Registration: performance guideline thresholds (Benaman et al. 2005; Setegn et al. 2010) and the scenario set were fixed in earlier work before these runs.

novelty_claims.quote: we used an innovative combination of three models
the present study is a novel contribution to the work being done to understand the potential for future changes
this research uses a novel setup of three different models

limits: The composition is none_fits: this is a scenario-projection study (calibrate and validate, then simulate scenarios) with no rival hypotheses, no crucial test and no later verification. Sub-claims: the model setup is capability_characterized (§5 ¶1); the provincial patterns (§3.4) are scenario estimates; the headline status estimate_with_resolution is a stretch, because uncertainty is shown only as interannual and GCM spread (Fig. 5) and no parameter sensitivity is tested. Inference: calibration and validation appear to use the same 1985-2000 gauge records (Table 3), so the gauge check is not held-out. The 'high degree of confidence' in projections (§4.1 ¶1) rests on baseline skill alone. Upstream model validations are cited from earlier work (Hoang et al. 2019; Triet et al. 2017), not redone. From the review: referee RC2's suggested resolution-aggregation test of the extent mismatch is not reported; the promised MERIT versus SRTM comparison and the Prek Kdam station do not appear in the final paper. Internal inconsistencies: the abstract says climate change decreases dry-season flows, while §3.2 ¶2 reports slight increases upstream from January to June; Phnom Penh baseline area is 188 km2 in §3.4 ¶1 but 118 km2 in Figure 7. The RC1 review text is truncated in the record; its comments are known only through AC3.
